claim: Megakaryocytes are the progenitor cells of blood platelets.
source: Megakaryocytes, the progenitor cells of blood platelets, play a crucial role in hemostasis by residing in the bone marrow and ensuring continuous platelet production.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational definition.

claim: Megakaryocytes reside in the bone marrow.
source: Megakaryocytes, the progenitor cells of blood platelets, play a crucial role in hemostasis by residing in the bone marrow and ensuring continuous platelet production.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Megakaryocytes do not enter the blood circulation intact.
source: Unlike other hematopoietic cells, megakaryocytes do not enter the blood circulation intact.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a distinguishing characteristic.

claim: Megakaryocytes remain anchored within the bone marrow while extending cytoplasmic protrusions called proplatelets through the sinusoidal endothelial barrier.
source: They remain anchored within the bone marrow while extending cytoplasmic protrusions called proplatelets through the sinusoidal endothelial barrier.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing megakaryocyte behavior.

claim: Proplatelets fragment into functional platelets.
source: These proplatelets subsequently fragment into functional platelets.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Laminin and collagen IV form three-dimensional ECM cages encompassing megakaryocytes.
source: Our findings reveal that laminin and collagen IV form three-dimensional (3D) ECM cages encompassing megakaryocytes and anchor them to the sinusoidal basement membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figures 1B-C.

claim: The ECM cages anchor megakaryocytes to the sinusoidal basement membrane.
source: Our findings reveal that laminin and collagen IV form three-dimensional (3D) ECM cages encompassing megakaryocytes and anchor them to the sinusoidal basement membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data showing connections between the cage and basement membrane.

claim: Laminin α4 exists in the ECM cage.
source: Gene deletion shows the existence of laminin α4 in the ECM cage that is necessary to maintain megakaryocyte-sinusoid interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with Lama4-/- mice shown in Figure 2.

claim: Laminin α4 is necessary to maintain megakaryocyte-sinusoid interactions.
source: Gene deletion shows the existence of laminin α4 in the ECM cage that is necessary to maintain megakaryocyte-sinusoid interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2E showing reduced sinusoid-associated megakaryocytes in Lama4-/- mice.

claim: Megakaryocytes actively contribute to ECM cage assembly.
source: Notably, megakaryocytes actively contribute to the ECM cage assembly; β1/β3 integrin knockout weakens these structures, increasing intravasation and entire megakaryocyte entry into circulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3 showing reduced ECM cage density in integrin knockout mice.

claim: β1/β3 integrin knockout weakens ECM cage structures.
source: Notably, megakaryocytes actively contribute to the ECM cage assembly; β1/β3 integrin knockout weakens these structures, increasing intravasation and entire megakaryocyte entry into circulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data in Figure 3D showing reduced laminin coverage.

claim: β1/β3 integrin knockout increases megakaryocyte intravasation.
source: Notably, megakaryocytes actively contribute to the ECM cage assembly; β1/β3 integrin knockout weakens these structures, increasing intravasation and entire megakaryocyte entry into circulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4B showing increased intravasation in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice.

claim: β1/β3 integrin knockout results in entire megakaryocyte entry into circulation.
source: Notably, megakaryocytes actively contribute to the ECM cage assembly; β1/β3 integrin knockout weakens these structures, increasing intravasation and entire megakaryocyte entry into circulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figure 4A, intravital imaging in Figure 4D-E, and lung data in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Inhibition of ECM proteolysis results in denser cage formation.
source: Inhibition of ECM proteolysis results in denser cage formation, increasing the frequency of immature megakaryocytes with impaired demarcation membrane system (DMS) development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6A-B showing increased collagen IV density with MMP inhibition.

claim: Inhibition of ECM proteolysis increases the frequency of immature megakaryocytes with impaired DMS development.
source: Inhibition of ECM proteolysis results in denser cage formation, increasing the frequency of immature megakaryocytes with impaired demarcation membrane system (DMS) development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by TEM data in Figure 6E-F showing increased stage II megakaryocytes.

claim: Megakaryocytes differentiate from hematopoietic stem cells.
source: Megakaryocytes, the precursors of blood platelets, differentiate from hematopoietic stem cells and mature in a complex bone marrow microenvironment.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Megakaryocytes are large, highly polyploid cells.
source: Megakaryocytes are large, highly polyploid cells that contain a complex invaginated network of membranes, known as the demarcation membrane system (DMS), which serves as a membrane reservoir for platelet production.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The demarcation membrane system (DMS) serves as a membrane reservoir for platelet production.
source: Megakaryocytes are large, highly polyploid cells that contain a complex invaginated network of membranes, known as the demarcation membrane system (DMS), which serves as a membrane reservoir for platelet production.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Megakaryocytes extend cytoplasmic protrusions called proplatelets through the sinusoidal endothelial barrier.
source: Instead, they remain anchored in the bone marrow and extend cytoplasmic protrusions called proplatelets through the sinusoidal endothelial barrier.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cited to previous work (Boscher et al., 2020; Stone et al., 2022).

claim: Proplatelets protrude into the lumen of bone marrow sinusoids where they undergo fragmentation to release individual platelets.
source: These protrusions protrude into the lumen of bone marrow sinusoids, where they undergo fragmentation to release individual platelets into the circulation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The remaining megakaryocyte cell body is ultimately phagocytosed in the stroma.
source: The remaining cell body, composed of a nucleus surrounded by a thin rim of cytoplasm, is ultimately phagocytosed in the stroma (Radley and Haller, 1983).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cited to Radley and Haller, 1983.

claim: Megakaryocytes are strategically located at the parasinusoidal region.
source: Megakaryocytes are strategically located at the interface between the bone marrow and the blood circulation, specifically at the parasinusoidal region (Lichtman et al., 1978; Stegner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cited to Lichtman et al., 1978 and Stegner et al., 2017.

claim: Megakaryocytes synthesize and release ECM components such as fibronectin, laminin, and type IV collagen.
source: Megakaryocytes actively influence their structural microenvironment through several ECM remodeling mechanisms, including the endocytosis of plasma proteins like fibrinogen, and the synthesis and release of extracellular matrix (ECM) components such as fibronectin, laminin, and type IV collagen (Abbonante et al., 2017; Handagama et al., 1987; Malara et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cited to Abbonante et al., 2017; Handagama et al., 1987; Malara et al., 2014.

claim: Megakaryocytes produce ECM-modifying proteins including MMPs, TIMPs, and LOX.
source: Additionally, they produce ECM-modifying proteins, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), and lysyl oxidase (LOX), which facilitate the continuous renewal and regulation of the matrix (Eliades et al., 2011; Malara et al., 2018; Villeneuve et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cited to Eliades et al., 2011; Malara et al., 2018; Villeneuve et al., 2009.

claim: Megakaryocytes remodel substrate-bound fibronectin matrix into basal fibrillar structures surrounding the cells.
source: Furthermore, we have recently discovered that megakaryocytes could remodel the substrate-bound fibronectin matrix into basal fibrillar structures surrounding the cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referencing prior work.

claim: The extent of fibronectin fibrillogenesis by megakaryocytes depends on substrate stiffness and relies on both β1 and β3 integrins.
source: The extent of fibrillogenesis depended on the stiffness of the substrate and relied on both β1 and β3 integrins (Guinard et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cited to Guinard et al., 2023.

claim: Essential components of the ECM surrounding megakaryocytes include collagen IV, fibronectin, fibrinogen, and laminin.
source: Numerous studies have identified essential components of this matrix, including collagen IV, fibronectin, fibrinogen, and laminin (Larson and Watson, 2006; Malara et al., 2014; Semeniak et al., 2016; Susek et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cited to multiple studies.

claim: Collagen I may inhibit proplatelet formation in vitro.
source: In vitro studies have shown that while collagen I may inhibit proplatelet formation, other ECM components, like collagen IV, fibrinogen, and fibronectin, can facilitate this process (Balduini et al., 2008; Malara et al., 2014; Sabri et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cited to Balduini et al., 2008; Malara et al., 2014; Sabri et al., 2004.

claim: Collagen IV, fibrinogen, and fibronectin can facilitate proplatelet formation in vitro.
source: In vitro studies have shown that while collagen I may inhibit proplatelet formation, other ECM components, like collagen IV, fibrinogen, and fibronectin, can facilitate this process (Balduini et al., 2008; Malara et al., 2014; Sabri et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and cited to Balduini et al., 2008; Malara et al., 2014; Sabri et al., 2004.

claim: Laminin γ1 chains delineate the basement membrane underlying the endothelium of sinusoids.
source: Our findings revealed that laminin ϒ1 chains and collagen IV delineated the basement membrane underlying the endothelium of sinusoids and the outer contour of mature megakaryocytes (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Aa).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1A.

claim: Collagen IV delineates the basement membrane underlying the endothelium of sinusoids.
source: Our findings revealed that laminin ϒ1 chains and collagen IV delineated the basement membrane underlying the endothelium of sinusoids and the outer contour of mature megakaryocytes (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Aa).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1A.

claim: Laminin γ1 and collagen IV delineate the outer contour of mature megakaryocytes.
source: Our findings revealed that laminin ϒ1 chains and collagen IV delineated the basement membrane underlying the endothelium of sinusoids and the outer contour of mature megakaryocytes (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1Aa).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1A.

claim: Fibronectin was detected in the basement membrane and around megakaryocytes.
source: Fibronectin was detected in the basement membrane and around megakaryocytes, while fibrinogen was more widespread, associated with the basement membrane, the megakaryocyte surface, and intracellular granules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ab-c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ab.

claim: Fibrinogen was associated with the basement membrane, the megakaryocyte surface, and intracellular granules.
source: Fibronectin was detected in the basement membrane and around megakaryocytes, while fibrinogen was more widespread, associated with the basement membrane, the megakaryocyte surface, and intracellular granules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ab-c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ac.

claim: Von Willebrand factor signal was restricted to the alpha granules of megakaryocytes.
source: Von Willebrand factor (VWF) signal was restricted to the alpha granules of megakaryocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ad).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ad.

claim: No detectable signals for type I and III collagen were observed around megakaryocytes or sinusoids.
source: We observed no detectable signals for type I and III collagen around megakaryocytes or sinusoids despite using antibodies validated on positive controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ae-f, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ae-f.

claim: Laminin γ1 and collagen IV form a reticular 3D ECM cage completely enveloping megakaryocytes.
source: Analysis of maximum Z-stack projections revealed that laminin ϒ1 and collagen IV formed a reticular 3D ECM cage completely enveloping megakaryocytes and extending radially from the sinusoidal basement membrane (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by 3D imaging in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The ECM cage extends radially from the sinusoidal basement membrane.
source: Analysis of maximum Z-stack projections revealed that laminin ϒ1 and collagen IV formed a reticular 3D ECM cage completely enveloping megakaryocytes and extending radially from the sinusoidal basement membrane (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by 3D imaging in Figure 1B-C.

claim: 92.8 ± 3.3% of megakaryocytes near sinusoids have a laminin cage.
source: Quantification showed that almost all megakaryocytes near sinusoids (sMK, 92.8 ± 3.3%) have a laminin cage, compared to only 11.4 ± 4.8% of megakaryocytes in the parenchyma (pMK; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Only 11.4 ± 4.8% of megakaryocytes in the parenchyma have a laminin cage.
source: Quantification showed that almost all megakaryocytes near sinusoids (sMK, 92.8 ± 3.3%) have a laminin cage, compared to only 11.4 ± 4.8% of megakaryocytes in the parenchyma (pMK; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Parenchymal megakaryocytes represent only 18 ± 1.3% of all megakaryocyte population.
source: Parenchymal megakaryocytes (pMK), which represented only 18 ± 1.3% of all megakaryocyte population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), were instead surrounded by a sparse thin network of laminin ϒ1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The ECM cage was present at all stages of megakaryocyte maturation.
source: The ECM cage was present at all stages of megakaryocyte maturation, including megakaryocytes with proplatelet extension (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging and quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I-J.

claim: After mechanical dissociation, 53.4 ± 5.6% of megakaryocytes retained their cages.
source: Remarkably, after mechanical dissociation and size exclusion, nearly half of the megakaryocytes successfully retained their cages (53.4 ± 5.6 %, 329 megakaryocytes counted from 3 mice), indicating strong physical attachments between both components (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 1D.

claim: Fibronectin and fibrinogen do not form a reticular ECM cage.
source: While fibronectin and fibrinogen are present around megakaryocytes and at the vessel-cell interface, they do not form a reticular ECM cage.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: No connection was found between fibronectin and fibrinogen deposition with the sinusoid basement membrane.
source: Furthermore, no connection was found between fibronectin and fibrinogen deposition with the sinusoid basement membrane, in contrast to the findings for laminin and collagen IV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Laminin α4 is abundantly found in bone marrow sinusoid basement membrane.
source: Among the γ1 chain-bearing laminin isoforms, laminin α4 was abundantly found in bone marrow sinusoid basement membrane (Susek et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and cited to Susek et al., 2018.

claim: Lama4-/- mice exhibit mild thrombocytopenia with platelet counts approximately 20% lower than wild-type mice.
source: These mice exhibit mild thrombocytopenia, with platelet counts approximately 20% lower than wild-type (WT) mice (Cai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results and cited to Cai et al., 2022.

claim: Platelets from Lama4-/- mice maintain normal ultrastructure and functions.
source: Their platelets maintain a normal ultrastructure and functions, as shown by flow cytometry and EM analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Bone marrow from Lama4-/- mice showed a normal number of mature megakaryocytes with characteristic ultrastructural features.
source: Bone marrow from Lama4-/- mice showed a normal number of mature megakaryocytes with characteristic ultrastructural features (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Megakaryocytes from Lama4-/- mice can extend proplatelets.
source: Analysis of bone marrow explants further demonstrated that these megakaryocytes could extend proplatelets, indicating preserved fundamental function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: In Lama4-/- mice, laminin γ1 deposition around megakaryocytes decreased by 1.7-fold compared to controls.
source: In Lama4-/- mice, laminin γ1 deposition around megakaryocytes and in the sinusoid basement membrane decreased by 1.7- and 2.6-fold compared to controls, indicating a disruption of the laminin cage (Figure 2A–B, upper panels).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 2B.

claim: In Lama4-/- mice, laminin γ1 deposition in the sinusoid basement membrane decreased by 2.6-fold compared to controls.
source: In Lama4-/- mice, laminin γ1 deposition around megakaryocytes and in the sinusoid basement membrane decreased by 1.7- and 2.6-fold compared to controls, indicating a disruption of the laminin cage (Figure 2A–B, upper panels).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 2B.

claim: Collagen IV organization remained unaltered around megakaryocytes in Lama4-/- mice.
source: However, collagen IV organization remained unaltered around the megakaryocytes in these mice (Figure 2A–B, lower panels), showing that laminin α4 is not necessary for collagen IV cage formation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 2B.

claim: Laminin α4 is not necessary for collagen IV cage formation.
source: However, collagen IV organization remained unaltered around the megakaryocytes in these mice (Figure 2A–B, lower panels), showing that laminin α4 is not necessary for collagen IV cage formation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2B showing normal collagen IV levels in Lama4-/- mice.

claim: Lama4-/- mice showed a 1.5-fold reduction in the number of megakaryocytes near sinusoids.
source: The total megakaryocyte density was similar to that of control mice (Figure 2D), but we observed more parenchymal MK with a 1.5-fold reduction in the number of megakaryocytes near sinusoids (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 2E.

claim: β1 integrin subunit is present on the plasma membrane and on the DMS of megakaryocytes.
source: Using conformation-independent antibodies, we showed the presence of β1 subunit on the plasma membrane and on the DMS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 3A.

claim: Total β3 integrins are present on the plasma membrane and on the DMS of megakaryocytes.
source: Similar findings were obtained for total β3 integrins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Activated β1 integrin is expressed only at interaction sites with laminin γ1 and collagen IV.
source: In contrast, the activated form of β1 integrin was expressed only at interaction sites with laminin γ1 and collagen IV, suggesting that activated β1 integrins mediate megakaryocyte interactions with the ECM cage (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 3B.

claim: Activated β1 integrins mediate megakaryocyte interactions with the ECM cage.
source: In contrast, the activated form of β1 integrin was expressed only at interaction sites with laminin γ1 and collagen IV, suggesting that activated β1 integrins mediate megakaryocyte interactions with the ECM cage (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by colocalization data in Figure 3B.

claim: Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice showed a 2.6-fold reduction in laminin γ1 deposition on the megakaryocyte surface.
source: Our analysis revealed a 2.6-fold reduction in laminin γ1 deposition on the megakaryocyte surface in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice compared to Pf4-Cre control mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 3D.

claim: Laminin γ1 forms a less dense network around megakaryocytes in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice with significantly increased mesh sizes.
source: Furthermore, intensity profiles demonstrated that laminin γ1 forms a less dense network around the megakaryocytes in the double knockout mice, with significantly increased mesh sizes (10.6±1.3 µm vs 6.3±0.6 µm, respectively; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 3D.

claim: The lower ECM density surrounding megakaryocytes in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice is not linked to increased matrix degradation.
source: Notably, this lower ECM density surrounding megakaryocytes in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice is not linked to increased matrix degradation or reduced laminin synthesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by gelatin degradation assay in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and laminin granule quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The lower ECM density surrounding megakaryocytes in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice is not linked to reduced laminin synthesis.
source: Notably, this lower ECM density surrounding megakaryocytes in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice is not linked to increased matrix degradation or reduced laminin synthesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by laminin granule quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The laminin γ1 network at the basement membrane remained unaffected in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice.
source: As expected, the laminin γ1 network at the basement membrane remained unaffected in these mice, as the integrin deletion is restricted to megakaryocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: There is a decrease in the expression of fibrillar fibronectin around Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes.
source: Further confocal and immunoEM examination revealed a decrease in the expression of fibrillar fibronectin around Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes, along with mislocalization of fibrinogen in the extracellular space of the DMS instead of the granules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Fibrinogen is mislocalized in the extracellular space of the DMS instead of the granules in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes.
source: Further confocal and immunoEM examination revealed a decrease in the expression of fibrillar fibronectin around Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes, along with mislocalization of fibrinogen in the extracellular space of the DMS instead of the granules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- platelets have intact α-granule secretion.
source: Flow cytometry showed that Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- platelets have intact α-granule secretion but impaired integrin-mediated aggregation, consistent with the bleeding phenotype observed in these mice (Janus-Bell et al., 2024; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- platelets have impaired integrin-mediated aggregation.
source: Flow cytometry showed that Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- platelets have intact α-granule secretion but impaired integrin-mediated aggregation, consistent with the bleeding phenotype observed in these mice (Janus-Bell et al., 2024; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice had a 50% reduction in platelet count.
source: As we previously described that Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice had a 50% reduction in platelet count (Guinard et al., 2023), we hypothesized that the organization of the ECM cage could contribute to the maturation process of megakaryocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and cited to Guinard et al., 2023.

claim: The number, size, and ploidy of megakaryocytes in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice are similar to control mice.
source: Firstly, the number, size, and ploidy of megakaryocytes in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice are similar to control mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, D, E.

claim: Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes show increased emperipolesis.
source: However, these mutant megakaryocytes show increased emperipolesis and severe DMS dysplasia, characterized by excessive membrane accumulation and abnormal architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TEM imaging in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes show severe DMS dysplasia characterized by excessive membrane accumulation and abnormal architecture.
source: However, these mutant megakaryocytes show increased emperipolesis and severe DMS dysplasia, characterized by excessive membrane accumulation and abnormal architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TEM imaging in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Typical platelet territories are poorly defined in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes.
source: Typical platelet territories are poorly defined, indicating disrupted maturation processes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TEM imaging in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 15.1 ± 2.7% of total bone marrow megakaryocytes were extending intravascular fragments in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice.
source: We found a significantly higher proportion of megakaryocytes that were extending intravascular fragments (i.e. intravasation) in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice (15.1 ± 2.7% of total bone marrow megakaryocytes) compared to that in Pf4Cre mice (2.9 ± 0.4% of total megakaryocytes).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: 2.9 ± 0.4% of total megakaryocytes were extending intravascular fragments in Pf4Cre mice.
source: We found a significantly higher proportion of megakaryocytes that were extending intravascular fragments (i.e. intravasation) in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice (15.1 ± 2.7% of total bone marrow megakaryocytes) compared to that in Pf4Cre mice (2.9 ± 0.4% of total megakaryocytes).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: Intact megakaryocytes were found in the sinusoid lumen in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice.
source: More strikingly, intact megakaryocytes were found in the sinusoid lumen, a rare phenomenon in control mice under physiological conditions (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 4A and quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: Intact Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes were not detected in the peripheral blood by flow cytometry.
source: Intact Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes were not detected in the peripheral blood by either flow cytometry or blood smear analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), indicating that megakaryocytes do not normally circulate in the systemic bloodstream.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Large MK nuclei were found trapped specifically in the lung capillaries of Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice.
source: Instead, large MK nuclei were found trapped specifically in the lung capillaries (Figure 4F–G), consistent with their known physical retention in the pulmonary circulation where they can release platelet.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging and quantification in Figure 4F-G.

claim: No significant change in the size of the endothelial pores was observed in Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice.
source: Furthermore, no significant change in the size of the endothelial pores (Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/-: 4.6±0.3 µm; Pf4Cre: 4.3±0.4 µm) was observed, indicating that increased megakaryocyte intravasion is not linked to endothelium alteration in mutant mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results with quantitative measurements.

claim: Most Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes did not spread and showed a round shape on immobilized laminin, fibronectin, or fibrinogen under static conditions.
source: Under static conditions, most Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- megakaryocytes did not spread and still showed a round shape on immobilized laminin, fibronectin, or fibrinogen (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by SEM imaging in Figure 5A and quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: Pf4-Cre megakaryocytes had capture yields of 70.5% on laminin.
source: Pf4-Cre megakaryocytes had capture yields of 70.5% on laminin, 83.6% on fibrillar fibronectin, and 82.0% on fibrinogen.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microfluidic adhesion assay data in Figure 5D.

claim: Pf4-Cre megakaryocytes had capture yields of 83.6% on fibrillar fibronectin.
source: Pf4-Cre megakaryocytes had capture yields of 70.5% on laminin, 83.6% on fibrillar fibronectin, and 82.0% on fibrinogen.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microfluidic adhesion assay data in Figure 5D.

claim: Pf4-Cre megakaryocytes had capture yields of 82.0% on fibrinogen.
source: Pf4-Cre megakaryocytes had capture yields of 70.5% on laminin, 83.6% on fibrillar fibronectin, and 82.0% on fibrinogen.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microfluidic adhesion assay data in Figure 5D.

claim: Itgb1⁻/⁻/Itgb3⁻/⁻ megakaryocytes experienced higher detachment rates across various ECMs under flow.
source: Pf4-Cre megakaryocytes remained anchored, while Itgb1⁻/⁻/Itgb3⁻/⁻ megakaryocytes experienced higher detachment rates across various ECMs (Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microfluidic data in Figure 5D and Videos 4 and 5.

claim: More megakaryocytes detached from Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- bone marrow tissue than Pf4-Cre explants after 3 hr.
source: After 3 hr, more megakaryocytes detached from Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- bone marrow tissue than Pf4-Cre explants, reaching a plateau at 6 hr.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 5F.

claim: β1 and β3 integrins control ECM-megakaryocyte interactions in their native bone marrow microenvironment.
source: These findings indicate that β1 and β3 integrins control ECM-megakaryocyte interactions in their native bone marrow microenvironment.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the bone marrow explant experiments.

claim: Treatment with batimastat and ilomastat increased the ECM density in megakaryocyte surrounding.
source: Regarding the cage, this treatment increased the ECM density in megakaryocyte surrounding, as evidenced by reduced fiber length and pore size (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 6B.

claim: MMP inhibitor treatment resulted in a significantly higher proportion of smaller megakaryocytes.
source: Remarkably, treatment with MMP inhibitors resulted in a significantly higher proportion of smaller megakaryocytes compared to untreated mice (white arrows in Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging and quantification in Figure 6C-D.

claim: 53.7% of megakaryocytes lacked the appropriate organization of the DMS in MMP inhibitor-treated mice.
source: We found that 53.7% of the megakaryocytes lacked the appropriate organization of the DMS in MMP inhibitors-treated mice, reflecting a primary failure in the cytoplasmic maturation (Stage II in Figure 6F right).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TEM analysis and quantification in Figure 6F.

claim: MMP inhibitor-treated mice showed a significant increase in the total megakaryocyte number compared to the control condition.
source: These mice also showed a significant increase in the total megakaryocyte number compared to the control condition (Figure 6D and F left), consistent with altered bone marrow ECM remodeling affecting megakaryocyte retention.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 6D and F.

claim: MMP inhibitors do not directly affect megakaryocyte maturation and density in vitro.
source: To assess whether MMP inhibition directly affects megakaryocyte maturation and density, we cultured primary megakaryocytes in the presence of increasing concentrations of inhibitors. We observed no significant change in proliferation, maturation, or proplatelet formation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by in vitro culture data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MMP inhibitor treatment resulted in upregulation of activated β1 integrin in bone marrow.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of bone marrow sections revealed an upregulation of activated β1 integrin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There was a significant reduction in megakaryocyte egress from the bone marrow microenvironment after 6 hr in MMP inhibitor-treated compared to control mice.
source: To further investigate this point, we quantified the number of megakaryocytes released from bone marrow explants. We observed a significant reduction in megakaryocyte egress from the bone marrow microenvironment after 6 hr in MMP inhibitor-treated compared to control mice (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 6H.

claim: MMPs are essential regulators of ECM homeostasis within the bone marrow.
source: Together, these results indicate that MMPs are essential regulators of ECM homeostasis within the bone marrow, influencing megakaryocyte maturation and attachment to the vascular niche.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the MMP inhibition experiments.

claim: The ECM cage is composed of laminin γ1 and α4 and collagen IV fibers.
source: This study identifies a 3D ECM cage anchoring megakaryocytes to bone marrow sinusoids. This cage, composed of laminin γ1 and α4 and collagen IV fibers, extends from the basement membrane and surrounds megakaryocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the main findings.

claim: Megakaryocyte integrin signaling regulates ECM cage remodeling and adhesive properties.
source: Megakaryocyte integrin signaling and ECM proteolysis regulate its remodeling and adhesive properties.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the main findings.

claim: ECM proteolysis regulates ECM cage remodeling and adhesive properties.
source: Megakaryocyte integrin signaling and ECM proteolysis regulate its remodeling and adhesive properties.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the main findings.

claim: The ECM cage is key for megakaryocyte positioning, maturation, and intravasation.
source: This dynamic microenvironment is key for megakaryocyte positioning, maturation, and intravasation, representing a novel concept in understanding physiological platelet formation (Graphical Abstract, Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the main findings and supported by the graphical abstract in Figure 7.

claim: Collagen I fibers were absent under steady-state conditions when analyzed using immunofluorescence and TEM.
source: Notably, when analyzed using immunofluorescence and transmission electron microscopy (TEM), collagen I fibers were absent under steady-state conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1Ae-f.

claim: GPVI-deficient megakaryocytes do not display alterations in ECM cage formation, vessel association, and intravasation behavior.
source: Furthermore, our findings indicate that GPVI-deficient megakaryocytes do not display alterations in ECM cage formation, vessel association, and intravasation behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: GPVI and α2β1 integrins are not critical for megakaryocyte function.
source: These observations support studies showing GPVI and α2β1 integrins are not critical for megakaryocyte function, underscoring potential redundancy in ECM-receptor interactions (Semeniak et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to Semeniak et al., 2019.

claim: ECM cage proteins may be derived from autocrine synthesis by megakaryocytes.
source: This indicates that the ECM cage proteins may be derived from autocrine synthesis and their production by neighboring cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the data showing intracellular laminin and collagen IV.

claim: ECM cage proteins may be produced by neighboring cells.
source: This indicates that the ECM cage proteins may be derived from autocrine synthesis and their production by neighboring cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the data showing ECM proteins in adjacent cells.

claim: The ECM cage is critical for positioning megakaryocytes near sinusoids.
source: Our findings in Lama4-deficient mice reveal that the ECM cage is critical for positioning megakaryocytes near sinusoids.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 2E showing reduced sinusoid-associated megakaryocytes in Lama4-/- mice.

claim: CXCL12/CXCR4 interaction mediates the parasinusoidal location of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow.
source: It is established that CXCL12 is a most potent physiological chemoattractant for megakaryocytes and that the parasinusoidal location of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow is mediated by the CXCL12/CXCR4 interaction (Hamada et al., 1998; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to Hamada et al., 1998 and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: The ECM cage is essential for maintaining megakaryocytes in the proximity of sinusoids.
source: Besides its potential role as a reservoir of such growth factors, we show that the ECM cage is also a crucial element in maintaining megakaryocytes in the proximity of sinusoids, which is essential for their efficient maturation and optimal platelet production.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the Lama4-/- mouse data.

claim: Megakaryocyte development occurs primarily at the sinusoid.
source: We also find the persistent presence of this ECM cage throughout megakaryocyte maturation, supporting previous findings that megakaryocyte development occurs primarily at the sinusoid (Gaertner et al., 2024; Lichtman et al., 1978; Stegner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to Gaertner et al., 2024; Lichtman et al., 1978; Stegner et al., 2017.

claim: β1 and β3 integrins are crucial for the building of the 3D ECM cages.
source: Our study highlights the indispensable roles of β1 and β3 integrins in maintaining megakaryocyte stability within the vascular niche. We demonstrate that these integrins are crucial for two fundamental processes: (1) the building of the 3D ECM cages and (2) the ECM-mediated adhesion mechanisms to the vascular niche.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the integrin findings.

claim: β1 and β3 integrins are crucial for ECM-mediated adhesion mechanisms to the vascular niche.
source: Our study highlights the indispensable roles of β1 and β3 integrins in maintaining megakaryocyte stability within the vascular niche. We demonstrate that these integrins are crucial for two fundamental processes: (1) the building of the 3D ECM cages and (2) the ECM-mediated adhesion mechanisms to the vascular niche.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the integrin findings.

claim: RhoA inhibition in Itgb1⁻/⁻/Itgb3⁻/⁻ megakaryocytes is likely contributing to the altered ECM remodeling.
source: For instance, RhoA inhibition in Itgb1⁻/⁻/Itgb3⁻/⁻ megakaryocytes (Guinard et al., 2023) is likely contributing to the altered ECM remodeling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to Guinard et al., 2023.

claim: No intravascular megakaryocytes were found in Lama4-deficient mice.
source: Of note, no intravascular megakaryocytes were found in Lama4-deficient mice, which have a normal collagen IV cage but a compromised laminin cage.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the data from Lama4-/- mice.

claim: The integrity of all components of the cage is not needed to keep megakaryocytes from entering circulation.
source: This indicates that the integrity of all components of the cage is not needed to keep megakaryocytes from entering circulation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from comparing Lama4-/- and Itgb1-/-/Itgb3-/- mice.

claim: Circulating megakaryocytes have been observed in human lungs during emergency megakaryopoiesis.
source: Importantly, circulating megakaryocytes have also been observed in human lungs during emergency megakaryopoiesis, such as in cases of infectious diseases, inflammatory conditions, and following cardiopulmonary bypass procedures (Frydman et al., 2023; Gelon et al., 2022; Puhm et al., 2023; Rapkiewicz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to multiple studies.

claim: Circulating megakaryocytes have been implicated in thrombotic complications.
source: These circulating megakaryocytes have been implicated in thrombotic complications, underscoring the importance of integrin signaling-dependent mechanisms regulating megakaryocyte retention and release.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to studies on circulating megakaryocytes.

claim: In Lama4⁻/⁻ mice, a collagen-rich ECM cage persists with normal fibronectin deposition.
source: In the Lama4⁻/⁻ mice, a collagen-rich ECM cage persists with normal fibronectin deposition, whereas the Itgb1⁻/⁻/Itgb3⁻/⁻ model displays a much more severe phenotype, characterized by the loss of both the laminin cage and collagen, along with the absence of fibrillar fibronectin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing the two mouse models.

claim: The Itgb1⁻/⁻/Itgb3⁻/⁻ model displays a severe phenotype characterized by the loss of both the laminin cage and collagen, along with the absence of fibrillar fibronectin.
source: In the Lama4⁻/⁻ mice, a collagen-rich ECM cage persists with normal fibronectin deposition, whereas the Itgb1⁻/⁻/Itgb3⁻/⁻ model displays a much more severe phenotype, characterized by the loss of both the laminin cage and collagen, along with the absence of fibrillar fibronectin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion comparing the two mouse models.

claim: MMPs profoundly influence megakaryocyte maturation by modulating the density of ECM cage architecture.
source: MMPs profoundly influence megakaryocyte maturation and their association with the vascular niche by modulating the density of ECM cage architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the MMP inhibition findings.

claim: In myelofibrosis, megakaryocytes secrete TGF-β1 which stimulates excessive ECM production by stromal cells.
source: In myelofibrosis, for instance, megakaryocytes secrete transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) which stimulates excessive ECM production by stromal cells (Abbonante et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to Abbonante et al., 2016.

claim: Pathological ECM accumulation in myelofibrosis leads to abnormally smaller megakaryocytes that exhibit reduced platelet production.
source: This pathological ECM accumulation leads to abnormally smaller megakaryocytes that exhibit reduced platelet production (Gianelli et al., 2023; Malara et al., 2018; Sarachakov et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to multiple studies.

claim: Proper megakaryocyte localization at the sinusoids depends on β1 integrin glycosylation.
source: Interestingly, previous research by K. Hoffmeister's group has demonstrated that proper megakaryocyte localization at the sinusoids depends on β1 integrin glycosylation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion referencing prior work.

claim: The absence of galactosylation in β4galt1-/- megakaryocytes leads to hyperactivity of β1 integrin, which negatively impacts the formation of the DMS.
source: Specifically, the absence of galactosylation in β4galt1-/- megakaryocytes leads to hyperactivity of β1 integrin, which negatively impacts the formation of the DMS (Giannini et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to Giannini et al., 2020.

claim: Integrin-mediated signaling and MMP proteolysis work together to regulate the density and cross-linking properties of the ECM cage.
source: Building on these insights, our study shows the coordinated interplay between integrin-mediated signaling and MMP proteolysis, working together to tightly regulate the density and cross-linking properties of the ECM cage and thereby control megakaryocyte maturation at the bone marrow-blood interface.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Despite effects on megakaryocyte maturation from MMP inhibition, no significant changes in circulating platelet counts were observed.
source: Intriguingly, despite these effects on megakaryocyte maturation, we observed no significant changes in circulating platelet counts, and importantly, platelet function remained preserved.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Platelet function remained preserved despite MMP inhibition effects on megakaryocyte maturation.
source: Intriguingly, despite these effects on megakaryocyte maturation, we observed no significant changes in circulating platelet counts, and importantly, platelet function remained preserved.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Megakaryocytes possess mechanosensing capabilities, primarily mediated by the β3 integrin subunit.
source: Notably, megakaryocytes possess mechanosensing capabilities, primarily mediated by the β3 integrin subunit, enabling them to detect and respond to changes in substrate stiffness (Guinard et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to Guinard et al., 2023.

claim: Both β1 and β3 integrins play essential roles in ECM fibronectin fibrillogenesis around megakaryocytes.
source: The assembly of extracellular matrix (ECM) fibronectin around megakaryopoiesis involves a more complex interplay of integrins, with both β1 and β3 integrins playing essential roles in fibrillogenesis (Abbonante et al., 2024; Guinard et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to Abbonante et al., 2024 and Guinard et al., 2023.

claim: The cooperative relationship between β1 and β3 integrins in fibrillogenesis appears to be conserved across various cell types.
source: This cooperative relationship appears to be conserved across various cell types (Attieh et al., 2017; Mets et al., 2019; Kyumurkov et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to multiple studies.

claim: The fibronectin matrix favors the deposition of other ECM proteins, such as collagens IV and various other glycoproteins.
source: Indeed, it is known that the fibronectin matrix favors the deposition of other ECM proteins, such as collagens IV and various other glycoproteins (Saunders and Schwarzbauer, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited to Saunders and Schwarzbauer, 2019.

claim: Integrin-mediated ECM interactions are crucial for platelet production, as demonstrated by the 50% reduction in platelet counts in integrin double knockout mice.
source: Overall, our findings reveal the supportive role of the ECM cage in platelet biogenesis. Integrin-mediated ECM interactions are clearly crucial, as demonstrated by the 50% reduction in platelet counts observed in integrin double knockout mice.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the findings.

claim: The ECM cage acts as a facilitator, optimizing the efficiency and precision of platelet production by guiding megakaryocytes to the right place at the right time.
source: In summary, the ECM cage acts as a finely tuned facilitator, optimizing the efficiency and precision of platelet production by guiding megakaryocytes to the right place at the right time.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a concluding statement.
